Arshi khan 3w Report this post India's startup funding fell 9% in H1 2026. The more useful story is where the money moved. Inc42's H1 2026 report puts total funding at $5.2B across 501 deals. Funding was down, but the number of deals actually went up 7%. The split by stage tells you why: → Late-stage funding fell 27% to $2.2B, and the median late-stage cheque dropped 68% to about $10M → Growth-stage funding rose 15% to $2.3B, with 33% more deals (190) → Seed funding rose 18% to $478M → AI startups raised $676M, a 317% jump Here's how I read it. Investors haven't stopped writing cheques. They're writing more of them, at smaller sizes, to companies that have already shown the model works. The big "raise now, figure out margins later" rounds are the ones getting squeezed. Public markets are pushing the same way. The report notes that roughly 75% of listed Indian startups are now profitable. That is the benchmark late-stage investors will hold private companies to. For founders, the takeaway is simple: proof comes before scale. Unit economics, payback period and a believable path to profit, shown in your own numbers, now matter more than a growth chart on its own. If you're building or joining a startup this year, what's the first metric investors or hiring managers ask you about? #Startups #IndianStartups #VentureCapital Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in

Arshi khan 1w Report this post India's startups raised about $2.9 billion between July and September. Bengaluru alone took 72.5% of it. That's from Entrackr's Q3 2026 report, and the headline number hides more than it shows. What stood out: • $2.9B across 266 deals, down from $3.5B in Q2 but up from $2.78B in Q3 2025 • 46 growth and late-stage deals took $1.89B; 194 early-stage deals shared $1.01B • Six startups listed. Six shut down. • AI ($635.3M) and EV ($583M) led the sectors The founder lesson, as I read it: capital hasn't disappeared, it has concentrated. Fewer than 50 growth and late-stage companies took most of the money, while nearly 200 early-stage startups split the rest in smaller rounds. If you're building right now, the useful question isn't "is the market open?" It's "what evidence (revenue, unit economics, a credible path to listing) will make me one of the 46, not one of the 194?" Founders and investors: what's the one metric you think gets a startup across that gap today? #Startups #VentureCapital #IndianStartups 1 1 Comment Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in

CS Abhishek Yadav 3w Report this post 𝐃𝐏𝐈𝐈𝐓 𝐒𝐄𝐑𝐈𝐄𝐒 | 01/07 🚨 𝐓𝐡𝐞 ₹200 𝐂𝐫𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐩 𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐊𝐧𝐨𝐰 If you thought DPIIT Startup Recognition was only relevant for early-stage startups, there’s an important 2026 update you should know. The Government has revised the Startup Recognition framework. The turnover threshold has increased from ₹100 crore to ₹200 crore. That means a startup can now have turnover of up to ₹200 crore in any financial year since incorporation and still satisfy the turnover criterion for DPIIT recognition, subject to the other eligibility conditions. But there’s more. For Deep Tech Startups: 🔹 Recognition period ➡️ up to 20 years 🔹 Turnover threshold ➡️ up to ₹300 crore For other startups, the recognition period remains 10 years from incorporation/registration. What does this practically mean? A company that may have crossed the old ₹100 crore threshold should not automatically assume that DPIIT recognition is out of reach anymore. But remember: ₹200 crore turnover alone does not make an entity a DPIIT-recognised startup. Other conditions relating to the entity, its age, innovation/scalability and its formation also need to be examined. So if your startup was previously considered ineligible only because of the ₹100 crore turnover limit, it may be worth reassessing your eligibility under the revised framework. AarambhGrow Group of Companies 40 followers 3w Report this post Building a startup? Don't miss the recognition that may matter. Most founders focus on product, funding and growth, and overlook one important step: DPIIT recognition under Startup India. For eligible startups, it can be a gateway to: ✅ Access to government benefits and schemes ✅ Growth opportunities through funding, mentorship and networking ✅ Being part of a larger Startup India ecosystem Not every business qualifies, so it helps to know where you stand early. Ask yourself: → Is your business registered as a Private Limited Company, LLP or Partnership Firm? → Is it built around innovation or a scalable business model? → Does it fall within the age and turnover limits for startups? Harsh Vardhan Singh Rawat 1w Report this post Indian startups raised more money this year. Fewer of them got any. Tracxn's numbers for 1 January to 21 September 2026: • Total funding is up 7%, to $10.3B • The number of funding rounds is down 38% • First-time funded companies are down 30% • Seed funding is down 37% Q3 on its own, per Inc42: $2.2B across 210 deals. Bengaluru took about 64% of it. Active investors fell 24%. In plain terms, the money hasn't gone anywhere. It's concentrating. There are fewer cheques, and they're going to companies that already look like they'll work. What that means if you're building at seed stage, especially outside Bengaluru: 1. Your first cheque is the hardest it's been in years. Plan for it to take longer than you think. 2. "Promising" isn't enough anymore. Revenue, pilots, a paying customer: that's what moves an investor in this market. 3. Use non-dilutive money first: government grants, incubator seed funds, challenge prizes like NESFIC's ₹20–40 lakh. They buy you the proof that makes a seed round easier. 4. Don't chase the hot sector just because it's hot. AI funding is up 265%, and 63% of investors in Inc42's survey already find AI valuations uncomfortable. At TBI GEU , the founders who raise aren't always the ones with the best pitch. They're the ones who show up with numbers. If you're raising in the next six months, what's been the hardest part so far? Mahesh K 2w Report this post The Startup India Seed Fund portal still loads. It stopped taking startup applications on 31 May. The portal's final notice gave 31 May 2026 as the last date for startups, and 30 June for incubators to finish selecting. As of 11 October I can find no new cycle announced. That is why I'm writing this. Plenty of guides still read like the scheme is open. The portal loads, the eligibility page loads, the checklist loads. You can spend a weekend on an application with nowhere to send it. If a new cycle is ever announced, these are the rules it ran on: DPIIT recognised, incorporated not more than 2 years before applying, and you could apply to 3 incubators at once. A portal that loads is not a scheme that is open. Tarun Dev Sinha 2w Report this post One week, Indian startups raised $411 million. The next, just $113 million. Did investors suddenly lose interest in startups? Not necessarily. Between October 5 and 10, 28 Indian startups raised $113.35 million. That's a drop of more than 72% from the previous week's $411.46 million. But look a little closer. The money didn't disappear completely. Early-stage startups raised $58.05 million across 22 deals. Growth-stage startups raised another $55.3 million across just 3 deals. And the week had some interesting stories: → DailyObjects raised nearly $35 million to expand its retail presence and product range. → Quanfluence , a photonic quantum technology startup, raised $10 million. → Beyond Appliances raised $11.4 million to grow its smart kitchen business. Different businesses. Different stages. Different reasons to raise money. Here's what I find interesting. A weekly funding number tells us how much money was invested. It doesnt tell us the whole story of where investors see potential. One week's total can change sharply because a few large deals happen, or don't happen. To understand the startup market, we need to look beyond the headline number: Which businesses are attracting capital? What stage are they at? And what are investors backing? Because a funding slowdown and a lack of investor interest aren't necessarily the same thing. What would you watch more closely: the total money raised, or the number and type of startups getting funded? 8 5 Comments Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in
